title: Let Kids Be Kids: When Collectibles Lose Their Playfulness
excerpt: There’s something unsettling about watching a child flip through a Pokémon card collection, only to see each card reduced to a dollar amount scribbled on a Post-it note attached to the sleeve of that card. The magic of those cards, the strategy of building a deck and the joy of battling friends seems to vanish when the only metric that matters is market value. Of course, the excitement of finding something rare is real, and if the kid is happy, that’s what counts. But when the game itself fades into the background, replaced by a spreadsheet mentality, you have to wonder: what’s the point? If no one is actually playing, if the cards are just tiny, untouchable assets, then what value do they truly hold? The soul of the game is in the playing, not the pricing.
content_html:
Back to overview

Card Collecting

There’s something unsettling about watching a child flip through a Pokémon card collection, only to see each card reduced to a dollar amount scribbled on a Post-it note attached to the sleeve of that card. The magic of those cards, the strategy of building a deck and the joy of battling friends seems to vanish when the only metric that matters is market value. Of course, the excitement of finding something rare is real, and if the kid is happy, that’s what counts. But when the game itself fades into the background, replaced by a spreadsheet mentality, you have to wonder: what’s the point? If no one is actually playing, if the cards are just tiny, untouchable assets, then what value do they truly hold? The soul of the game is in the playing, not the pricing.

Video Games

The same unease creeps in with video game collecting. There’s a growing trend of games sealed in shrink wrap, locked away in acrylic cases (tombs!) for experiences that were meant to be lived. For me, a physical game is a passport to adventure. I play it, I beat it, I let it earn its place on my shelf as a trophy of time well spent. If it doesn’t deliver, I pass it on to someone who might enjoy it more. But when games become museum pieces, untouched and unopened, they stop being games at all. They become investments, relics, or status symbols. The irony is that the more we treat these things as sacred objects, the less we actually use them for their intended purpose: to bring joy, to connect, to play.

The Cost of Collecting

I’m not judging anyone’s collecting hobbies here, if you’re an adult, it’s your money, and if creating little tombs of video games brings you joy, then by all means, carry on. But we do have to acknowledge that this collecting behavior fuels a more extreme problem: scalping. When rare or nostalgic items become financial assets rather than sources of fun, it can price out the very people who might cherish them most: kids who just want to play.

I remember going on a two-week bike-packing trip across France about a decade ago. For entertainment, I brought along a Game Boy Color and a handful of games. I tossed them into a bag with an extra set of batteries, and that was it, no protection needed and no second thoughts on the impact if something got lost or damaged. Now that I know some of those games have skyrocketed in value, I might not make the same choice today. But honestly? I’d be happier if the market for old games hadn’t spiraled into this endless cycle of price hikes. The joy of discovery and the simplicity of play shouldn’t come with a hefty price tag.

content_html_zh:
Back to overview

卡片收集

看着一个孩子翻阅神奇宝贝卡片系列，却发现每张卡片都被简化为一张纸条，写在卡片套上的便利贴上，这让人感到有些不安。 当唯一重要的衡量标准是市场价值时，这些卡牌的魔力、构建套牌的策略以及与朋友战斗的乐趣似乎都消失了。 当然，发现稀有东西的兴奋是真实的，如果孩子高兴，那才是最重要的。 但当游戏本身淡出背景，取而代之的是电子表格心态时，你不得不想：这有什么意义？ 如果没有人真正玩，如果牌只是微小的、不可接触的资产，那么它们真正具有什么价值？ 游戏的灵魂在于玩法，而不是定价。

电子游戏

同样的不安也出现在电子游戏收藏中。 用收缩包装密封、锁在亚克力盒子里的游戏越来越流行（坟墓！） 寻找那些本该经历的经历。 对我来说，实体游戏是冒险的通行证。 我玩它，我打败它，我让它在我的书架上赢得一席之地，作为一个值得花时间的奖杯。 如果它没有交付，我会将其传递给可能更喜欢它的人。 但当游戏成为博物馆的藏品、未经碰触、未打开时，它们就不再是游戏了。 它们成为投资、文物或地位的象征。 讽刺的是，我们越是把这些东西视为神圣之物，我们就越少真正将它们用于其预期目的：带来欢乐、联系、玩耍。

收集成本

我不是在这里评判任何人的收集爱好，如果你是成年人，那是你的钱，如果创造电子游戏的小坟墓给你带来快乐，那么无论如何，继续吧。 但我们必须承认，这种收集行为引发了一个更极端的问题：倒卖。 当稀有或怀旧的物品成为金融资产而不是乐趣的来源时，它可能会让最珍惜它们的人（只想玩耍的孩子）付出代价。

我记得大约十年前，我曾进行过一次为期两周的自行车穿越法国旅行。 为了娱乐，我带了一台 Game Boy Color 和一些游戏。 我把它们扔进一个袋子里，里面还有一组额外的电池，就这样，不需要保护，也不需要再考虑东西丢失或损坏时的影响。 现在我知道其中一些游戏的价值已经飙升，我今天可能不会做出同样的选择。 但说实话？ 如果老游戏市场没有陷入这种无休止的价格上涨循环，我会更高兴。 发现的乐趣和游戏的简单性不应该伴随着高昂的价格标签。
